I found this game called Endless Legend, returning to strategy games for a bit from FPSs and MMOs. It's ... interesting. It's a very nuanced and subtle game, if you like those sorts of things. It's on PC. I'll not give away everything, as there are a lot of interesting little bits, but:

It's a 4X strategy with turn-based city management like Civ, but you also have roaming armies with heroes that go on quests. Quests typically come from indigenous clans on the map, of which there are many and most can be pacified then assimilated into your empire. There is a combat interface that opens right on the map itself, which is really nice as it lets you maneuver to take advantage of the terrain to great effect. Combat is also turn-based, and if not resolved at the end of 6 turns, results in a draw.

The city building is a touch boring for me. You have to construct boroughs to get your city to really grow, and buildings are almost all geared toward industry and production. The city interface itself is very similar to what's in Civ. The biggest difference though is that each city controls one region with set borders--there can only be one city per region. So far I find that having beyond 2-3 cities/regions gets unwieldy, but the cities also get quite large (bigger than I would normally feel comfortable having in a game like Civ) and producing settlers negatively impacts citizen happiness. Cities can also come under siege.

You can set an Empire Plan, which is supposed to be the infrastructure that shapes domestic and foreign policy. There is a pretty straight forward tech tree where you do research. The diplomacy is a bit nebulous, and the negotiation interface is not very intuitive. You have a hero and unit market, in addition to what your cities and assimilated clans can produce. You also have a workshop for heroes and armies, wherein you can change equipment and appearances.

Different ages that your empire enters depending on achievements. There are 8 factions you can play. I have played with all 8 of them, and find some easier than others to work with. They're all very different, though.

Complex, but a pretty cool game. Wondering if anyone else is/has played it and what you think of it?

The factions, for anyone interested:

Wild Walkers - Elven/Druid inspired faction. They get bonus industry from tiles with forest on them and their heroes (if specialized to be governors) boost food and industry production. They can see when enemies are in their territory, even through fog of war and are really good at building cities.

Broken Lords - Humans who have been cursed to go without physical bodies, and instead their souls are bound to suits of armor (Alphonse Elrich style). Because they don't have organic bodies, they get no benefit from food/cannot naturally regenerate, and instead have to spend dust (equivalent to gold in Civ) to increase their population or heal their units. The ability to pay to heal units combined with the natural stats of the Stalwart (their infantry unit) makes them extremely durable.

Necrophage - A hive-mind faction consisting of humans who died while infected with a specific parasite that causes them to transform into insect/human hybrids. They have a major penalty to food production, but for every 8 units that die in combat they're involved in (whether ally or enemy) they get a food stockpile that they can spend for a large, 1-time food boost in a city. Their units spread disease in other armies, and their Proliferator unit can infect new victims so they become Necrophage when they die in battle. They also get a bonus to their attack stat for each faction they're currently at war with, and are incapable of peace/alliance.

Vaulters - A group of tech-worshipping explorers who delve beneath the planet's surface looking for ancient technologies. They're science- and strategic resource-focused. They can designate any of the 6 strategic resources as their holy resource (and can change it mid-game, as well). Their units get double the stats from gear made of their holy resource, they get a serious boost to holy resource output during winter, and can spend their holy resource to teleport units between cities.

Ardent Mages - All magic users, the Ardent Mages are the other science-focused faction. Their units have really high base damage, and do more damage the lower their health is. Unfortunately, their units are also some of the most fragile. Their primary unique features are spells and pillars. Pillars are aura nodes that provide some kind of buff for a certain number of turns; they can increase science, dust, influence, or food output on nearby tiles, and there's one that increases the movement speed of nearby units. Spells are abilities you can use in combat (once per battle, I believe) that can do things like stun enemies or buff friendly units.

Drakken - A faction of dragons/dragonspawn that considers themselves the caretakers of the planet. They have unrivaled influence output, which allows them to dominate the diplomatic game (also they can spend extra influence to force other factions into truces/peace/alliances with them). All their units have the Fast Learner trait, which gives them +50% xp from all sources. Drakken armies are usually small but obnoxiously leveled up, and a properly leveled-up general can give them massive amounts of hp. Played correctly, Drakken are even harder to kill than the Broken Lords, but the BL's ability to heal instantly puts them in the top spot, defense-wise.

Roving Clans - Nomads and the other dust-focused faction. They can uproot their cities and move them around, which allows for a lot of possibilities. You can settle a city in an area rich in food and industry to get it started, then move it to a more dust-rich area, or move a fully established city to a strategically vulnerable area instead of trying to settle a new one there. See a huge enemy army approaching? Just pack up your city and leave. The only faction that starts with the market unlocked, the Roving Clans' massive dust production (particularly from trade routes) allows them to completely dominate the market, driving up prices so high that no one else wants to pay them (and even if they do, the Clans get a cut!).

Cultists - The other influence-focused faction, the cultists are only allowed to have one city. However, by converting the villages of neutral monsters (called minor factions) to their religion, they gain converts (free extra citizens), free military units, and extra food/industry/science/dust/influence output from the tiles surrounding the villages. The villages also function as garrisons and provide vision. The Cultists are also the only faction who can level their city districts to level 3 (others can only reach level 2), which increases the districts' outputs.

The Forgotten - (Note this is a DLC faction that I don't have) A faction that is incapable of producing science. Instead, they have the ability to steal techs from rival factions and buyout techs with dust. They also have several other abilities that make them better at espionage and pillaging than the other factions.
